stories.headline: Flights near normal as ground stop inquiry turns to two routers and a funding fight
stories.summary: Air travel was largely back to normal on Monday, three days after a nationwide ground stop halted U.S. departures for more than four hours. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said investigators are examining two recently installed routers, President Trump blamed the Biden administration in his first comments and pressed Congress for more money, and Democrats said the FAA has not spent what it already has. The FAA is preparing to brief Congress.
stories.why_it_matters: Thanksgiving travel starts next week, and Duffy would not promise that a similar failure cannot happen again. How much more taxpayers spend on air traffic control, and who oversees it, is now a fight between the White House and a Congress that Democrats are about to control.
stories.background: The FAA runs air traffic control over a network of radar, radio and data links, much of it decades old. On Friday, Nov. 13, communication problems across several sites led the agency to hold departing flights nationwide, which officials called the longest such stop in 25 years. Duffy has tied the failure to maintenance work by contractor L3Harris on an older telecommunications system. Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to modernize the system, and Duffy asked in September for $30 billion more. Democrats won control of Congress in this month's midterm elections and take over in January.

facts.text: Air travel was largely returning to normal on Monday, though some disruption continued as airlines worked to get back on schedule.

Duffy said investigators are analyzing two routers installed in recent weeks at FAA facilities in Arkansas and Texas.
Duffy said there were no signs of a foreign cyberattack, Fox News reported.

Aviation experts and federal officials told The New York Times that the outage began after a new piece of networking equipment flooded the rest of the system with data, and that the underlying cause is unclear.
In his first public comments on the ground stop, Trump blamed the Biden administration for the FAA's aging systems and urged Congress to approve more funding.
Administration officials asked for $50 billion for air traffic control, CBS News reported.
Congress approved $12.5 billion last year to upgrade the air traffic control system, and Duffy asked in September for another $30 billion.
Democrats said the FAA has not spent money Congress already approved, and Duffy rejected that criticism.
Duffy declined to apologize for the ground stop and, when asked, could not guarantee that a similar failure would not happen again.
Officials said the ground stop was not related to the FAA's new $875 million AI-based system for predicting problems in the airspace.
The FAA is preparing to brief Congress on the failure, CNN reported.

stories.headline: Federal prosecutor warns Sen. Warren of legal consequences over planned Trump-related probes
stories.summary: Aaron Reitz, a U.S. attorney in Texas, sent Sen. stories.background: Democrats won control of Congress in this month's midterm elections, which gives them committee chairmanships and subpoena power starting in January. Several have said they plan to investigate Trump and people around him. U.S. attorneys are the Justice Department's top federal prosecutors in each district. stories.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is facing growing scrutiny from lawmakers in both parties and from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over how his department handled Nvidia and its AI chip exports. stories.summary: Federal investigators said on Sunday that a preliminary finding shows the tanker Atlantic Asphalt lost steering shortly before it struck the docked river cruise ship American Heritage in New Orleans on Friday. stories.why_it_matters: Tankers and tourist boats share a crowded stretch of the Mississippi in the middle of a city. The finding points investigators toward equipment and maintenance rather than the weather or the cruise ship.
stories.background: The Atlantic Asphalt hit the American Heritage while the cruise ship was docked on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday, Nov. 13. Passengers, crew and two police officers ended up in the river, and no one was killed. The National Transportation Safety Board, which investigates serious marine accidents, is leading the inquiry. Preliminary findings can change; a final report usually takes a year or more.

Trump wants to rebuild it as a championship-level course, one of several changes he has pursued in the capital. stories.headline: Iran targets a US base in Bahrain for the second time in three days
stories.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it launched six drones on Sunday at a US air defense radar at the Riffa base in Bahrain, the second attack on the Gulf state in three days. Bahrain said it intercepted the attacks before they reached their targets. A US aircraft carrier arrived in the region the same day, while Iran said a path to a deal with Washington remains open.
stories.why_it_matters: The strikes end a roughly two-month pause in Iranian attacks on Gulf states and come as US-Iran peace talks appear stuck, raising the risk of renewed fighting in a region that supplies much of the world's oil.
stories.background: The United States and Israel launched a war on Iran in February, and Iran has since fired missiles and drones at Gulf states that host US forces. Bahrain is home to the US Navy's Fifth Fleet. Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum in June outlining an end to hostilities, according to Gulf News, but attacks continued through the summer before a lull that began in September. Talks on a final deal now appear to have stalled, and the US carried out limited strikes on Iran's Qeshm island in recent weeks, CBS News reports.

stories.headline: Yemen's government pulls troops from Red Sea strait as Houthis close in on Aden
stories.summary: Yemen's internationally recognised government said it was withdrawing its last forces from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to defend Aden, its interim capital. Military and government sources said Houthi fighters had advanced to within 60 kilometres of the city. The pullback leaves the strait, a gateway to the Red Sea and Suez Canal, under Houthi control.
stories.why_it_matters: Bab el-Mandeb is one of the world's main shipping chokepoints, so who holds it affects freight costs and the price of goods far from Yemen. A fall of Aden would leave the Saudi-backed government without its seat.
stories.background: Yemen has been at war since the Iran-backed Houthi movement seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014 and a Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 to back the government, which now sits in the southern port of Aden. The front was largely frozen for years but reopened during the wider regional war that began in February. stories.headline: Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge in its largest drone barrage of the war
stories.summary: Ukraine launched more than 1,300 drones at Russia overnight, striking the bridge that links Russia to occupied Crimea. The Kremlin called the damage minor, while Crimea's Russian-installed governor said traffic was being limited. The attack followed a weekend of Russian strikes on Ukraine's power and rail networks, and US-brokered peace talks that ended without a breakthrough.
stories.why_it_matters: Both sides are escalating long-range strikes as winter begins and talks stall, which means more blackouts for Ukrainians and a war that looks no closer to ending.
stories.background: Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and has repeatedly bombed its power grid before winter. The Crimean Bridge, opened in 2018 after Russia annexed Crimea, is a supply route for Russian forces and has been hit several times. Ukraine's drone units rely on Starshield satellite links, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said since mid-October that speed limits imposed on the terminals are making it harder to shoot down Russian drones, European Pravda reported. A round of US-brokered peace talks recently ended without agreement.

stories.headline: Congo's Ebola outbreak still out of control after six months, Africa CDC says
stories.summary: Africa's main public health agency said on Sunday that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo remains out of control six months after it was declared. More than 11,000 cases have been recorded and nearly half of those infected have died. The agency cited deadly attacks on health workers, unpaid staff and a shortage of resources.
stories.why_it_matters: This is already the deadliest of Congo's Ebola outbreaks and is on course to pass the death toll of the 2014-16 West African epidemic. The longer it runs, the greater the chance of spread across borders.
stories.background: Ebola is a severe viral disease spread through contact with the body fluids of infected people. This outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain, was declared in May in Congo, a country that has now had 17 Ebola outbreaks. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control lists it as a multi-country outbreak. Health agencies say armed conflict, displacement, hunger and mistrust of health workers in the affected areas have made it hard to trace and treat cases.

facts.text: The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said on Sunday the outbreak was still out of control six months after it was declared, citing deadly attacks on health workers, unpaid staff and a lack of resources.
More than 11,000 cases have been recorded and nearly half of those infected have died, according to government data.

It is the deadliest of Congo's 17 Ebola outbreaks and is on track to surpass the toll of the West African outbreak that killed about 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016, the Associated Press reported.

The World Food Programme said about 5,400 deaths have been reported, that children account for more than a quarter of confirmed cases and a third of deaths, and that seven in 10 children under five with confirmed Ebola have died.
Africa CDC said services have been brought closer to affected communities but that conflict and displacement continue to fuel the outbreak.

stories.headline: China confirms first Xi-Trump-Putin summit, set for Thursday in Shenzhen
stories.summary: China's foreign ministry confirmed that President Xi Jinping will host US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a three-way meeting in Shenzhen on Nov. 19. stories.headline: Tech stocks slide again as Nvidia earnings and Anthropic's IPO loom
stories.summary: A selloff in technology shares carried into a new week, with S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures lower Monday morning after fresh losses in Asian artificial-intelligence stocks. Investors are waiting for Nvidia's quarterly results on Tuesday, its first since chief executive Jensen Huang stepped down, and for the pricing of Anthropic's initial public offering, which Bloomberg says is expected Wednesday with trading to start Thursday.
stories.why_it_matters: AI-linked companies make up a large share of the stock indexes that most retirement accounts and index funds track, so a prolonged drop in them shows up in ordinary savers' balances. This week's two events are being treated as a test of whether investors still want to pay high prices for AI growth.
stories.background: Much of the stock market's rise in recent years has come from a handful of companies tied to artificial intelligence, with chipmaker Nvidia the largest of them. Nvidia's shares have fallen sharply amid allegations that its chips were diverted to China and the resignation of its longtime chief executive, Jensen Huang. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, is about to sell shares to the public for the first time in what outlets describe as a very large offering. Separately, U.S. Treasury yields rose last week after inflation data and comments from Federal Reserve officials led traders to consider the possibility of interest-rate increases. The Nasdaq Composite ended Friday down about 6% over the past month, while the S&P 500 was down about 2%.

facts.text: S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures fell Monday morning ahead of Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's market debut.
The decline followed new weakness in Asian AI-related stocks, and Bloomberg reported that emerging-market stocks had their largest drop in more than a week.
Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, Nov. 17; the company said in a securities filing that the date was unchanged after its chief executive's departure.
Anthropic's IPO is expected to price on Wednesday and begin trading on Thursday, according to Bloomberg.
U.S. Treasury yields fell Monday after rising significantly last week on inflation data and Federal Reserve officials' comments, the Wall Street Journal reported.
The dollar index (DXY) rose to 103.533, which the Wall Street Journal described as a 19-month high.
Gold edged up but stayed near one-year lows after losing 4.5% last week, according to the Wall Street Journal.
Economist Jason Furman, a former White House adviser, said that if AI turns out to be a bubble that bursts, the most likely result is a 25% drop in the broader market, MarketWatch reported.
Morgan Stanley strategists, in their outlook for the year ahead, recommended raising stock holdings to the highest possible allocation, MarketWatch reported.

stories.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that Nvidia should look outside the company for a successor to Jensen Huang, who has resigned as chief executive, and called for a "dramatic shakeup" of its leadership. Nvidia has named its finance chief, Colette Kress, interim CEO. The company reports earnings Tuesday and, according to the New York Post, has 10 days to answer the administration's questions about banned chip sales.

stories.headline: Japan's economy shrinks unexpectedly as energy costs squeeze households
stories.summary: Japan's economy contracted at an annualized rate of 0.1% in the July-September quarter, a preliminary government estimate showed Monday. Japan imports nearly all of its oil and gas, so it is exposed when energy prices rise, as they have since the war involving Iran disrupted supplies. concept.explanation: GDP is the total value of the goods and services a country produces in a period, and it is the broadest single measure of whether an economy is growing or shrinking.
